title: Infrastructure as Code Scanning
summary: Infrastructure as code scanning is the automated static analysis of declarative infrastructure and configuration definitions, such as cloud resource templates, Kubernetes manifests, container build files, serverless definitions and policy bundles, looking for misconfigurations that would create security exposure when the code is applied. Because infrastructure definitions are machine-readable and describe the intended end state, scanners can reason about them far more reliably than they can reason about application logic, checking properties such as publicly reachable storage, permissive identity policies, unencrypted data stores, containers running as privileged or as root, absent network policies, disabled audit logging and hard-coded registry credentials. The category is closely related to cloud security posture management, with the key distinction that posture management assesses what is deployed while IaC scanning assesses what is about to be deployed, which is why it belongs in the pull request and in the pipeline before apply or sync. For a practising engineer the practical difficulty is drift and context. A scanner cannot see values injected at deploy time from a variable file, cannot know that a resource is internet-facing by design in a specific environment, and cannot tell whether an exception was granted deliberately. Effective programmes express policy as code with the same review process as application code, use environment-aware rule sets, classify findings by whether they affect a trust boundary, and detect drift between the repository and what the provider actually reports. Common failure modes are scanning only a subset of repositories, ignoring modules and nested templates, allowing unbounded inline suppressions, and treating a clean scan as evidence that the deployed environment is compliant.
objectives: You will be able to explain how static analysis of infrastructure definitions differs from cloud posture assessment of deployed resources.
You will be able to identify high-impact misconfiguration classes in cloud templates, Kubernetes manifests and container builds.
You will be able to integrate IaC scanning into a pull request and pipeline gate before apply or sync operations run.
You will be able to write policy as code with severity, environment scope and an exception process that expires.
You will be able to explain why variable interpolation, modules and cross-stack references produce scanner blind spots.
You will be able to describe how to detect drift between committed infrastructure code and the resources actually deployed.
